sections.text: To calculate a percentage increase or decrease, subtract the old value from the new value, divide the result by the old value, and multiply by 100. A positive answer is an increase and a negative answer is a decrease. A price that moves from 25 to 30 gives (30 - 25) / 25 x 100 = +20%, and a price that moves from 50 to 40 gives (40 - 50) / 50 x 100 = -20%. The rest of this guide covers the three situations where people go wrong: reading rates in percentage points, reversing a percentage, and chaining several changes.

The test score result is 18.0556% before rounding, shown here to two decimal places. The last row shows why a large percentage can mislead: a rise of 2 units on a base of 1 is +200%, while a rise of 4,000 on a base of 50,000 is only +8%. Always quote the absolute change alongside the percentage when the base is small.

Going from 50 to 75 is a 50% increase. Going back from 75 to 50 is a 33.3% decrease, not 50%, because the base is now 75. This asymmetry is the source of most percentage arithmetic errors. The table shows how large a rise you need to recover from a fall.

When a quantity is itself a percentage, such as an interest rate or a pass rate, there are two different ways to describe a change. A rate moving from 4% to 5% rose by 1 percentage point, but its relative increase is (5 - 4) / 4 x 100 = 25%. A rate moving from 3.5% to 4.25% rose by 0.75 percentage points, which is a relative increase of 21.4%. A rate moving from 10% to 15% rose by 5 points, or 50%. A headline that says a rate "rose 2%" is ambiguous, so check whether the writer means points or relative change before you use the figure.
Reverse percentages: finding the original value

If you know the new value and the percentage change, divide the new value by (1 + rate) for an increase, or by (1 - rate) for a decrease. A salary of 54,000 after an 8% raise was 54,000 / 1.08 = 50,000. A bill of 1,260 after a 10% reduction was 1,260 / 0.90 = 1,400. The shortcut of subtracting the percentage from the new value is wrong: 10% of 1,260 is 126, and 1,260 + 126 = 1,386, not 1,400. The reason is that the percentage was taken from the original value, so you must divide back through the same multiplier.

Successive percentage changes multiply; they do not add. Convert each change to a multiplier, multiply them, then subtract 1. Three yearly rises of 10% give 1.10 x 1.10 x 1.10 = 1.331, a total rise of 33.1%, not 30%. A rise of 20% followed by a rise of 30% gives 1.2 x 1.3 = 1.56, so 56%. A fall of 20% followed by a fall of 30% gives 0.8 x 0.7 = 0.56, a total fall of 44%. A rise of 50% followed by a fall of 50% gives 1.5 x 0.5 = 0.75, a 25% net loss, which shows that averaging the two changes to get 0% is incorrect.

Percent change treats one value as the original, so it has a direction. Percent difference is used when neither value is the original, and one common convention divides the gap by the average of the two values. For 50 and 75, the gap is 25 and the average is 62.5, so the difference is 40%, while the percent change from 50 to 75 is 50%. The two numbers answer different questions. Which convention applies depends on the field, so state the formula you used.

items: Dividing by the new value instead of the old one. The old value is always the denominator.
Forgetting to multiply by 100, which leaves a decimal such as 0.2 instead of 20%.
Calculating a change from zero. The formula divides by zero and has no answer, so report the absolute change.

Using percent change when the old value is negative. The calculator on this site divides by the absolute value of the old number, so a move from -50 to -25 shows as +50%. That convention is debated, so describe such results in words as well.
Quoting a huge percentage from a tiny base without the underlying numbers.
